cleanupOnUninstall.description:
Run a post-delete cleanup Job on `helm uninstall` that removes the leftovers
the worker creates at runtime but Helm does not manage: the Kueue / Node Feature
Discovery / CSI Helm releases, their CRDs, the finalizers pinning Kueue and
Instance objects, and the aggregated APIServices / webhooks. Disabled by default
because those CRDs may be shared with other workloads; enable only when this
release exclusively owns them (e.g. CI / e2e).

certmanager.description:
Configure cert-manager integration for every serving certificate this release needs: the
worker's webhook certificate and Kueue's. It lives under `global` because Kueue is a vendored
subchart and `global` is the only channel Helm gives a subchart to this chart's values. Each
component used to be switched on its own, so a cluster with cert-manager installed issued the
worker's certificate through it while Kueue went on self-signing — two answers to one question,
and the detection behind `auto` could never reach Kueue at all.

enabled.description:
Whether to issue the serving certificates with cert-manager. Accepts a string (or the
equivalent boolean): "auto" creates the cert-manager resources only when the cert-manager
CRDs are detected in the cluster; "true" always creates them (cert-manager must be
installed); "false" never creates them and each component generates and manages its own
certificate.

Turning it ON later is a plain `helm upgrade`. Turning it OFF again is not: cert-manager
owns the Secret Kueue's chart wants to template and writes CA bundles Helm never recorded,
so `helm upgrade` refuses the Secret before it starts, and forcing past that fails
mid-apply on the visibility APIServices. docs/migration/to-subcharts.md carries the
sequence that does work. The same applies when cert-manager is uninstalled from a cluster
while this is "auto", which flips the answer without anyone editing a value.
enabled.title: enabled

manufacturers.description:
Accelerator manufacturers to manage, one row per manufacturer holding everything the
release needs to know about it. `pciVendorID` is what NFD labels its devices with,
`resourceName` what its device-plugin advertises to the kubelet, `runtimeName` the
RuntimeClass its workloads run under, and `partitionKind` its own name for hardware
partitioning ("mig" is NVIDIA's name for the concept, not the concept's). Each of those
four is also a `pkg/nodefeature` default overridable by a `GPUSTACK_<MANUFACTURER>_*`
variable, and this chart fans every stated one out as that variable to the worker and to
the device-managers — so a row here decides them rather than restating them, and a field
left out keeps the operator's own default. `runtimeInjectsDriver` is the exception, a
deployment fact no Go code holds: it marks a manufacturer whose user-space driver reaches
a container only through its container runtime, so that manufacturer's device-manager runs
under the RuntimeClass too. Every other vendor's device-manager reads its management
library from a hostPath mount the DaemonSet already makes.

`runtimeInjectsDriver` — not `runtimeName` — is also what decides which RuntimeClasses this
chart creates (`deviceManager.createRuntimeClasses`). The two differ on purpose:
`runtimeName` is the class the operator will USE for a vendor, while
`runtimeInjectsDriver` is the only case where the runtime's presence can be inferred, since
such a vendor's accelerators cannot work at all unless its container toolkit registered the
handler. Every other vendor's device plugin needs no RuntimeClass, so the handler may well
be absent while its accelerators work — and creating one there would break them: the
operator attaches a RuntimeClass to a workload whenever one exists, so the kubelet would
reject every Pod of that vendor for a runtime nothing configured. A class the vendor's own
operator created is still used; this chart just never conjures one.

The keys are the manufacturer list: they become the worker's `--manufacturer` flag (which
is where the `gpustack-cpu-info` NodeFeatureRule's vendor IDs come from, since the worker
renders that rule itself), one device-manager DaemonSet each, and Kueue's credits mapping.
Each DaemonSet only schedules on nodes NFD labelled with the matching PCI vendor, so
adding a row is all it takes for a new vendor's devices to be labelled, detected and given
a device-manager, and a row no node in the cluster carries simply runs nothing.

It lives under `global` because the vendored Kueue subchart reads it too, and `global` is
the only channel Helm gives a subchart to this chart's values. The defaults are every
manufacturer `pkg/nodefeature` knows, which a Go test asserts. Narrow the list by setting a
row to `null` — an unwanted row is otherwise harmless (its DaemonSet schedules on no node),
so this is about how much a release renders, not about what works.
manufacturers.title: manufacturers

apiVersion: config.kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta2
kind: Configuration
featureGates:
  AssignQueueLabelsForPods: false
  TASBalancedPlacement: true
  # Enables resources.quotaCheckStrategy below (alpha in Kueue 0.18). The bundled
  # controller image is always 0.18, so the gate is always available.
  QuotaCheckStrategy: true
health:
  healthProbeBindAddress: :8081
metrics:
  bindAddress: :8443
# enableClusterQueueResources: true
webhook:
  port: 9443
leaderElection:
  leaderElect: true
  resourceName: c1f6bfd2.kueue.x-k8s.io
controller:
  groupKindConcurrency:
    Job.batch: 5
    Pod: 5
    Workload.kueue.x-k8s.io: 5
    LocalQueue.kueue.x-k8s.io: 1
    ClusterQueue.kueue.x-k8s.io: 1
    ResourceFlavor.kueue.x-k8s.io: 1
clientConnection:
  qps: 50
  burst: 100
#pprofBindAddress: :8083
#waitForPodsReady:
#  timeout: 5m
#  recoveryTimeout: 3m
#  blockAdmission: false
#  requeuingStrategy:
#    timestamp: Eviction
#    backoffLimitCount: null # null indicates infinite requeuing
#    backoffBaseSeconds: 60
#    backoffMaxSeconds: 3600
#manageJobsWithoutQueueName: true
# The namespaces Kueue manages jobs in. Deliberately unset: the chart renders the
# default as every namespace but kube-system and this release's own, which is what
# lets the release install into any namespace — Kueue refuses to start when this
# selector matches the namespace it runs in, and a subchart value cannot be
# templated. State it to take the default over, and own that rule.
#managedJobsNamespaceSelector:
#  matchExpressions:
#    - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
#      operator: NotIn
#      values: [ kube-system, gpustack-system ]
integrations:
  frameworks:
  - "batch/job"
  - "kubeflow.org/mpijob"
  - "ray.io/rayjob"
  - "ray.io/raycluster"
  - "jobset.x-k8s.io/jobset"
  - "trainer.kubeflow.org/trainjob"
  - "kubeflow.org/paddlejob"
  - "kubeflow.org/pytorchjob"
  - "kubeflow.org/tfjob"
  - "kubeflow.org/xgboostjob"
  - "kubeflow.org/jaxjob"
  - "workload.codeflare.dev/appwrapper"
  - "pod"
  - "deployment"
  - "statefulset"
  - "leaderworkerset.x-k8s.io/leaderworkerset"
#  externalFrameworks:
#  - "Foo.v1.example.com"
#fairSharing:
#  preemptionStrategies: [LessThanOrEqualToFinalShare, LessThanInitialShare]
#admissionFairSharing:
#  usageHalfLifeTime: "168h" # 7 days
#  usageSamplingInterval: "5m"
#  resourceWeights: # optional, defaults to 1 for all resources if not specified
#    cpu: 0    # if you want to completely ignore cpu usage
#    memory: 0 # ignore completely memory usage
#    example.com/gpu: 100 # and you care only about GPUs usage
resources:
  # Kueue is not the authoritative ledger in this operator — the Devices CR
  # is. A ClusterQueue advertises exactly one coarse admission dimension (cpu
  # for general pools, the manufacturer credits for accelerated pools), while a
  # Workload still carries the Pod resources the queue does not cover: memory
  # and ephemeral-storage on every pool, cpu on accelerated pools, and the
  # node-level .sliced.* counters the scheduler/kubelet read. Check only the
  # covered dimension and ignore the rest, instead of refusing to assign a
  # flavor for an uncovered resource (which would mark the Workload inadmissible).

  # `resources.transformations` is absent here on purpose: the chart renders it from
  # `global.manufacturers`, mapping every accelerator resource key onto that
  # manufacturer's single credits resource so a queue can carry one credit budget. It
  # is not stated in this string because a user copying the string to change one
  # feature gate would silently drop the mapping the whole scheduling chain rests on.

#objectRetentionPolicies:
#  workloads:
#    afterFinished: null # null indicates infinite retention, 0s means no retention at all
#    afterDeactivatedByKueue: null # null indicates infinite retention, 0s means no retention at all
controllerManagerConfigYaml.description:
Kueue's controller_manager_config.yaml, delivered through the manager-config
ConfigMap. Two keys are absent on purpose and rendered by this chart instead, because
Helm merges a subchart's values rather than templating them: `resources.transformations`,
the credits mapping derived from `global.manufacturers`, which a user copying this string
must not be able to drop silently; and `managedJobsNamespaceSelector`, whose default
follows the release namespace. Everything else is maintained here, and a selector stated
here still wins.
controllerManagerConfigYaml.title: controllerManagerConfigYaml

migrate.description:
Migration hook Jobs. A pre-install/pre-upgrade Job reaps a Kueue left stranded by an
interrupted teardown, and on an upgrade applies the vendored subcharts' CRDs, which Helm
itself applies on install only. A post-upgrade Job retires the release records of the
per-application releases these subcharts replaced and prunes what they left behind. Both run
the operator image, which bundles kubectl, helm and this chart; `helm upgrade --no-hooks`
skips them.

image.description:
Per-hook image overrides (`repository`/`tag`/`pullPolicy`); unset keys fall back to the
chart-level `image`. Overridable so an upgrade is never blocked by an operator tag that is
not mirrored yet — at the cost that the CRDs the hook applies are then the ones vendored by
the image it does run.
image.title: image

affinity.description:
Affinity for the NFD master, and the only way to spread its replicas across nodes: NFD
renders no topology spread constraints. Stated here because a spread knob a user cannot find
in this file is a knob that does not exist, and because replacing it wholesale is what
setting it does.

It is NFD's own default — a preference for control-plane nodes — with one deliberate change:
the role label is matched with `Exists` rather than `In [""]`. That label's value is a
convention, not an API: kubeadm and kind set it empty, k3s and RKE2 set it to "true", so a
value test silently matches nothing on those and the preference quietly stops existing.
`Exists` is also what every other control-plane matcher in this file uses, tolerations and
both CSI drivers included. Being stated pins the rest of the block: re-read NFD's default
when bumping the subchart, as with every image tag here.
affinity.title: affinity

restrictions.description:
What the NFD master is allowed to write. Every value here restates an NFD default,
stated because the whole chain depends on it: labels, taints, annotations and extended
resources all stay enabled, an existing label may be overwritten, and the labels a
NodeFeature asks for are honoured — that last one is how a device-manager's detections
reach its node.

`nodeFeatureNamespaceSelector` is deliberately absent. Pinned to one namespace it makes
the master ignore every NodeFeature created anywhere else, which is exactly what taking
over a cluster's existing NFD must not do: a vendor GPU operator keeps its NodeFeatures
in its own namespace, and they are the features being adopted. Unset means every
namespace, so — together with the two permissive keys above — a NodeFeature anywhere can
influence node labels; `denyNodeFeatureLabels` is the lever that tightens it.

enable.description:

not `enabled`.

replicaCount.description:
Number of NFD master replicas. The master is what turns a device-manager's detections into
node labels, so while it is down no node is ever (re)classified and the scheduling chain
stalls for new or changed nodes. Above one, NFD's own chart adds `-enable-leader-election`
for you; the standbys watch without writing. NFD's templates render no topology spread
constraints, so spreading these replicas across nodes means setting `master.affinity` below —
which replaces NFD's own preference for control-plane nodes rather than adding to it.

worker.description:
High availability. Every control-plane component this chart deploys elects a leader, so extra
replicas stand by instead of sharing the work: they buy failover, not throughput. A highly
available install raises the replica count of each one and enables the disruption budget that
goes with it — `worker`, `kueue.controllerManager`, `node-feature-discovery.master`, and the
`controller` of both CSI drivers. Spreading those replicas across nodes is per-component and
each key below says what its component supports; the cluster needs as many schedulable nodes as
the largest replica count for a hard spread to be satisfiable. Everything else here is a
DaemonSet, one pod per node already. docs/operation/high-availability.md walks through it.

affinity.description:
Affinity for the worker, replacing the default `preferred` pod anti-affinity that keeps
replicas off one node without ever making one unschedulable.
affinity.title: affinity

dataDir.description: Host path mounted at /var/lib/gpustack for persistent operator data.
dataDir.title: dataDir

disableApplications.description:
Applications the worker must not install at runtime, or `*` for all of them. This chart
deploys every one of them itself, so the default takes the worker out of that business
entirely. Keep the wildcard: whenever this chart deploys the worker, anything left off the
list makes the worker install a SECOND release of this same chart, whose render overlaps this
one's. Helm refuses an object another release owns, so that install fails and the worker's
startup with it. Handing a component back would mean disabling it here and in this chart's
own switch for it, in step, through every upgrade — nothing checks that, which is why the
supported split is all or nothing. The worker installs applications only where no chart
deploys it (see docs/architecture.md, "Two install modes"). The value is
templated rather than appended through `extraArgs` because the flag accumulates across
occurrences, so a second one could only ever disable more. Accepted names: `*`, `kueue`,
`node-feature-discovery`, `csi-driver-nfs`, `csi-driver-s3`, `device-manager`.
disableApplications.title: disableApplications
